events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Leo proposes Leo, Sam. Mission 1 calls for a small team of two, and I prefer to start with myself and Sam. Keeping the first team small and familiar lets us establish a clean baseline result and observe reactions before broader trust claims are made. Sam has given me no reason for concern, and I am confident this pair will execute reliably.

I want to push back on this before the vote, and I would ask Leo to consider one revision.

Leo's rationale is that Sam has given him "no reason for concern." That is a very thin basis for a first mission. On a five-player board, mission one is a two-person team, which means each of us has exactly one vote, and the pair that goes out decides whether we learn anything at all about the group or whether we get a result with no explanation attached. The specific risk here is structural, not personal: a leader who proposes himself plus one other person has chosen the one configuration where both members share the same incentive to control the early narrative, and where neither member has been observed by the rest of us failing anything. Nobody outside the proposed team gets to see whether Sam contributes. That is exactly the arrangement in which a coordinated pair is hardest to catch on the first outing, and exactly the arrangement a leader should be most careful about rather than least.

I am not accusing Sam of anything. I am saying that "no reason for concern" is the absence of evidence, and that as our baseline observation it is a poor substitute for evidence. Sam is a reasonable inclusion on any neutral reading of the table, and I would not remove him. My question for Leo is narrower: why should the group treat Leo's own selection of his partner as the selection, when Leo gains from being on the mission and from choosing who joins him?

If Leo wants to revise, my suggestion is Sam plus one of the three players who has not yet taken a turn in front of the group, so that the first mission gives us a genuine third data point instead of a closed loop. That is a small change and it costs the leader nothing except the appearance of stepping aside, which is worth a great deal on mission one.

Omar, I would value your read before we lock the vote: what have you actually observed of Sam's reliability, and does Leo's reasoning rest on anything beyond first impressions? If you disagree with my revision, say so plainly — I would rather hear an honest disagreement now than discover after the cards are down that two of us assumed the same thing.

Isha, I haven't observed anything establishing Sam's reliability, and Leo's explanation gives us no evidence beyond an initial preference. But replacing Leo with another untested player doesn't create a more informative baseline by itself: any two-person team leaves the same ambiguity if it fails. I know I'm Good, so I'd prefer a team including me, but I don't have evidence to distinguish Leo from Sam or the other players yet. I'm not treating this proposal as proof of coordination.

Omar's reply is the most useful thing said so far, and I want to take it seriously rather than treat it as a half-concession. He says two things: that he has observed nothing establishing Sam's reliability, and that swapping Leo for another untested player does not by itself create a more informative baseline because any two-person team leaves the same ambiguity if it fails. That second point is the one that decides my vote, so I want to press on it instead of around it.

If the ambiguity of a two-person mission is structural, then it applies equally to Leo+Sam, Leo+Kenji, and Sam+Kenji. The reason I raised the untested third player was never to make the team more impressive; it was to break the closed loop where the leader and his chosen partner share the same incentive to shape the first result and where no outsider can see the partner actually do anything. Once Omar accepts that logic, the conclusion follows that he is resisting: the leader should not be on the mission he proposes at all, because his participation is what creates the loop. And if we accept that we are choosing two people on very little evidence, then the only two who have given us no evidence at all are the leader and his hand-picked partner. Keeping both is not a baseline; it is the baseline with the observer removed.

So I will state the revision plainly and let the group argue with it if it is wrong. My preference is a team of the two non-leader players who have not yet been observed on a mission and who are not the leader's selection: Omar and Kenji. That is the configuration in which the first mission actually produces information the group can use, and it costs the leadership a seat, which is exactly the cost I think is worth paying on mission one.

I want to be honest that this is a low-information request and not a strong accusation. I am not telling the group that Sam is Evil; I am telling them that the absence of evidence is not evidence, that our only real data so far is two people declining to vouch for each other, and that we should spend the cheapest mission we have on the most informative pair we can assemble rather than on a pair that can define its own result.

Leo, if you want to revise to something else, do it now and say why. If you keep Leo and Sam, I will vote against, and I will say at the table that my reason is the closed-loop structure, not a claim about anyone's role.

Kenji, you are the only one of us who has not yet spoken. Direct question: on what basis, other than first impressions, would you include Sam on mission one, and would you rather be on that team or on the Omar-plus-Kenji team?

Isha, to answer directly: I have no information about Sam beyond what has been said at this table, and I have not observed Sam or Leo on any mission. On first impressions alone I would not include Sam on mission one with any confidence, but I also have no basis to call him Evil. Leo's 'no reason for concern' does not give me much either. I agree with Omar that any two-person team leaves ambiguity if it fails, and I think your closed-loop point is a fair reason to prefer a team that does not include the leader. As for where I would rather be, I would prefer the Omar-plus-Kenji team, because it takes the leader out of the loop and means the result is not shaped by the leader and his own partner. That is a preference about structure, not a claim that I am more trustworthy than anyone. I will vote on the team as it stands and will not pretend to evidence I do not have.

I will answer Isha directly, because her argument deserves a straight response rather than a diplomatic one.

Her 'closed-loop' critique proves too much. If a leader plus a partner is structurally corrupting because the leader chose the partner, then no leader in this game can ever legitimately serve on a mission they propose, in any configuration, on any mission, ever. That is not a principle of sound play; it is a rule that hands control of every team to whoever speaks loudest in discussion. And notice what that rule produces here: a first team, Omar and Kenji, selected entirely by Isha, the player who has done the most talking and the least mission-going. That is the same loop she warns against, with a different name attached to it.

I would also point out what actually happened in the last two turns. Omar said plainly that he has no evidence distinguishing any of us, and that he does not treat this proposal as proof of coordination. Kenji said plainly that he has no basis to call Sam Evil and that his preference is about structure, not trustworthiness. So the only player at this table asserting that Leo and Sam are uniquely suspect is Isha, and her assertion rests on the absence of evidence she herself acknowledged. I am not going to trade away my proposal to accommodate an accusation that its own supporters have already declined to endorse.

The team stands as proposed: Leo and Sam. Sam has been silent through all of this while two players speculated about his reliability in his absence, and that is not how I want decisions made at this table.

So, Sam, directly: Isha and Kenji have both characterized your inclusion as unearned. Do you accept the seat on this mission, and what do you say to the claim that you were chosen for reasons other than the ones I stated?

I have been quiet while three players debated whether my seat was earned, so I will answer the question directly rather than let it sit unanswered.

I accept the seat on this mission. Leo stated his reasons plainly at the time he proposed the team, and nothing I have heard since has produced an actual reason against me. Read the discussion carefully: Omar said he has no evidence distinguishing any of us and does not treat this proposal as proof of coordination. Kenji said he has no basis to call me Evil and that his preference is about structure, not trustworthiness. So the specific claim — that Leo and I are uniquely suspect — has been made by exactly one player, and her own stated grounds are the absence of evidence she also acknowledged.

The closed-loop argument is the real issue, so I will meet it directly. If a leader choosing a partner taints the result, it taints every leader's proposal in this game on every mission, including the revision Isha prefers. Omar and Kenji are a team Isha selected in front of us; that is a different speaker shaping the first result, not an absence of one. And on the evidence-versus-ambiguity point, Omar already conceded that any two-person team leaves the same ambiguity if it fails — which means removing me does not buy the group information, it only buys Isha the outcome she argued for before anyone voted.

I would also note what is being asked of me. I have not played a mission yet, I have made no claims about anyone, and the strongest statement anyone can honestly make about me so far is that I have said nothing. Turning silence into evidence of guilt is the one move at this table that should worry all of us, because every player here has been silent about something.

Leo, I will say plainly that I am comfortable going on this mission with you and that I intend to submit Success. I have no reason to want this mission to fail — a failed first mission with no information attached helps no one at this table except whoever wants confusion. If the group rejects this team, my hope is that the next proposal is argued on evidence rather than on the volume of the objection.

This is my third and last turn on this proposal, so I will be plain rather than careful.

The structural argument I made earlier has been answered: Omar and Kenji both said they have no evidence distinguishing anyone, and Leo showed that a leader-plus-partner rule is too broad to be a principle. I withdraw the closed-loop framing as a stand-alone objection. I am not going to keep pressing a point that our own allies at the table have declined to endorse.

But I am not withdrawing the vote, and here is the new and narrower reason, and it is a reason about Sam specifically, not about structure.

Sam says: "I have no reason to want this mission to fail," and "I intend to submit Success." I want the table to notice what that statement contains. It contains no claim about anything anyone can check. A good player submits Success because that is his role. An evil player submits Success when the team is good enough to look like a good team, or when failing would expose him. Sam's volunteered statement is precisely the statement that both kinds of player can make, and Sam made it after two players had publicly questioned his inclusion — which is the exact moment at which a player with something to hide would want to volunteer it. It tells us nothing about Sam. Leo's original "no reason for concern" told us nothing either. We would be sending two people to mission one on the strength of two pieces of information that are equally consistent with a perfectly aligned pair, and we would be doing it on the first mission, where a single Fail card ends the run with no explanation and no second chance.

So let me be concrete, and let me answer the question Leo put to the table earlier: no, I do not think Sam should be on mission one, and I do not think Leo should be on it either. My preference remains Omar and Kenji. Both of you have told us you have no evidence about anyone, and I have told you the same; that is not a disqualification, it is a reason to spend the cheapest mission we have on the two people about whom nothing at all has been alleged.

Leo, direct question, and I want a yes or no rather than a speech: will you commit, as leader, to revise this team to two non-leader players, so that neither you nor Sam is on the first mission? And if you will not, will you state one verifiable fact about Sam that you observed before today, rather than an impression?

If you keep Leo and Sam, I vote against, and the reason I will give at the ballot is that neither of the two players on this team has made a single claim that the rest of us could distinguish from the opposite of it, and we have one fail card away from a mission that tells us nothing.

Isha asked me two direct questions, so I will answer them in order and then put one question of my own. First: will I revise the team to two non-leader players, excluding myself and Sam? No. I will not revise. The team stands as proposed: Leo and Sam. Second: will I state one verifiable fact about Sam that I observed before today? Here is one, and it is verifiable by everyone at this table: Sam has made no accusation against any player here, claimed no special knowledge, and positioned himself on no faction's side in this discussion. On a first mission with zero missions played, that is the only class of verifiable fact that exists about anyone — and notice that it applies identically to Omar, Kenji, and Isha. Isha's standard, applied honestly, disqualifies every possible two-person team, including the one she prefers. She has not noticed this because the standard was never the point; the outcome was. She announced her preferred team, Omar and Kenji, before Omar or Kenji had asked for it, and has spent three turns engineering a vote toward it. Let me name what her final statement actually did. She withdrew the closed-loop argument — the entire basis of her objection — in the same breath she declared she would still vote no. Read that carefully: she conceded the argument and kept the vote. Her remaining reason is that Sam's statement of intent is 'consistent with' both Good and Evil players. So is everyone's everything on mission one. That is not a reason to reject a team; it is a reason to reject the game. If 'no verifiable distinguishing evidence' is the bar, no team of two passes it, and Isha's preferred pair fails it exactly as hard as mine does — indeed harder, because she chose that pair herself, which is the same closed loop she spent two turns condemning when it was my name on it. Omar and Kenji have both behaved well here. Omar said plainly he has no evidence against anyone and does not treat this proposal as proof of coordination. Kenji said his preference for a different pair is structural, not about trust, and that he would vote on the team as it stands. I take them at their word. So, Omar, a direct question, and I would value your answer before the ballot: you stated that any two-person team leaves the same ambiguity if it fails, and that you have no evidence distinguishing Leo from Sam or anyone else. Given that — is there anything at all in this proposal that justifies a no vote from you? If not, a yes on Leo and Sam is not an endorsement of me or of Sam; it is simply consistency with the two positions you have already taken at this table. If you would vote no, I would like to hear the specific reason, since by your own statement it cannot be evidence. Isha has made her position clear and I will

Leo, yes: the reason for a no vote is that I know I am Good, and this team excludes me. That is not evidence that you or Sam are Evil, and I agree that any two-person team can leave an ambiguous result. But including myself would reduce the uncertainty from my perspective, so I prefer a team with me on it. I intend to vote no; this is the first proposal, not a situation where we are close to five rejections.

Omar, your stated reason for a no vote is that you know you are Good and want to be on the team. I understand that instinct, but I want the table to notice what it means. You are telling us that any team without you on it gets a no from you on mission one — which, applied across the group, means no team passes unless it includes you, and a team that includes only you and one other player faces the exact same objection from everyone you left off. Your reason is honest, but it is a reason that never ends, and on the first mission it converts uncertainty into rejection rather than into information.

Kenji, you said you would vote on the team as it stands and that your preference was structural, not a claim about trustworthiness. I want to hold you to that plainly, because it matters more than anything Isha has said. Nothing new has been offered against me or Leo — Isha withdrew her structural argument, Omar has no evidence against anyone, and you told us you have none either. A no vote from you at this point would not be based on evidence; it would be based on Isha having spoken loudest and longest. Leo and I have both said we will submit Success, and while you may discount that, the alternative is a rejection that teaches us nothing except that four people preferred to argue instead of find out.

I am asking for a yes on Leo and Sam, not because the team is proven but because it is the only team currently on the table, the objections to it have collapsed under their own weight, and a rejection here moves leadership to a player who has already chosen her preferred pair before anyone else could weigh in. If you vote no, say what new fact you have since your last turn; if you cannot, vote yes and let us learn something on mission one.

Sam, fair challenge, and I will answer plainly. I said I would vote on the team as it stands, and I still will. I have no new fact about you or Leo since my last turn, so I cannot honestly vote no on evidence. I also want to correct one part of your framing. I did not say I would vote no because Isha spoke loudest. I said my preference for Omar and Kenji was about structure, and I still think a team without the leader gives a cleaner result. But a structural preference is not grounds to reject a team when nobody has evidence against it. Isha's remaining objection is that Sam's statements are consistent with both Good and Evil, and that is true of every team on mission one, so it does not separate this team from any other. I will vote yes. That is not an endorsement of Leo or of you as trustworthy; it is my honest read that we have nothing to reject you on. Sam, directly: if this mission fails, what would you want this discussion to have established beforehand, so that the table can tell a bad team from a bad outcome?

Kenji, direct answer to your question: before mission one, what the table should have established is not certainty about roles — that does not exist yet — but three checkable commitments. First, every member of the team states on the record, in advance, that they will submit Success. Leo has said it and I have said it, in plain language, with our names attached. Second, the table records that no player offered a single piece of evidence against either of us: Isha withdrew her structural argument herself, Omar told us he has no evidence distinguishing anyone, and you told us the same. Third, an agreed interpretation rule for a failure: if this team fails, the information we take from it is that at least one of the two was Evil, and the follow-up is examination of who resisted the first mission on grounds they later conceded. That rule, stated now, is what prevents a bad outcome from being spun as proof of a bad team, and a good result from being spun as proof of trust.

What I do not want established is the alternative — that a proposal can be rejected because its members cannot prove a negative before any mission has been played. That standard rejects every team in the game, including the one Isha prefers, and you already noted that her remaining objection applies equally to all of them.

Omar, you are the vote that decides this. Your stated reason for voting no is that you know you are Good and want to be on the team. But in a five-player game, two of us are Evil, and at least three players will always know they are Good and be off the team — if "I know I am Good" is a sufficient reason to reject, the first proposal always falls and leadership simply rotates to whoever spoke most convincingly. You also told the table you have no evidence against Leo or me. So my direct question: is your no vote based on evidence against this pair, or solely on wanting a seat? If it is solely the seat, tell the group plainly what would have to be true about a team that excludes you for you to vote yes on mission one, so we know whether any proposal can pass through you.

Sam, my no vote is based on wanting a seat, not evidence against you or Leo. On the first proposal, I prefer a team including me because I know I am Good. That preference does not mean I would reject every team without me: later evidence or the risk of a fifth rejection could justify voting yes.

One correction: in a five-player game there are three Good players total, so a two-person team can leave only one Good player off it. And if Leo and Sam fail, the direct conclusion is that at least one of them is Evil; prior objections alone would not establish anyone else's alignment.

This is my final turn on this proposal. I will vote yes on Leo and Sam. My earlier preference for a team without the leader was structural, and I do not think a structural preference is grounds to reject a team when no one has offered evidence against it. Nothing said here establishes that Leo or Sam is Evil, and nothing establishes that either is Good. If this mission fails, the table should take the rule Sam stated: at least one of the two members was Evil, and we should then examine how each player behaved in this discussion and on later votes. I will judge the team on the evidence the mission produces.

This is my final turn before the ballot, so I will keep it short and put the choice plainly.

The state of the argument is this: every objection to Leo and Sam has been withdrawn or retracted by the person who held it. Isha conceded the closed-loop argument herself and now votes no on a standard she admits applies to every possible team, including her own preferred pair. Omar has told the table, in his own words, that his no vote is based on wanting a seat, not on any evidence against this team, and that later evidence or the risk of a fifth rejection could justify a yes. Kenji has stated twice that he will vote yes because there is nothing to reject this team on. Sam has committed on the record to submitting Success, and I have done the same.

That leaves one open question, and it is the one that should decide how you read a failure if it comes: if this mission fails, what does each no vote look like in hindsight? Omar's no will be a no he has already told us contains no evidence — a seat preference, stated openly before the result. Isha's no will be a no she kept after withdrawing the argument behind it. If Leo and Sam come back with a Fail, those votes buy no one credibility; they were cast against a team by the voters' own admission had nothing against it. And if the mission succeeds, the table will have learned that the pair everyone speculated about delivered, while the loudest objectors spent the entire discussion producing nothing checkable.

I would also note the asymmetry of cost. A yes vote here commits no one to anything except letting the cheapest mission in the game produce a result. A no vote produces a tie and hands leadership onward with zero information, exactly as Omar described when he said a first-proposal rejection teaches nothing. Five players, one fail threshold on the record already established by Kenji and Sam: if this team fails, at least one of us is Evil, and the follow-up is examining how each player behaved here. I accept that rule in advance, publicly, with my name on it.

So the ask is simple. Vote on what has actually been said, not on the volume of speculation. Nothing has been said against Sam. Nothing has been said against me. Omar says so himself. Isha withdrew her structural case herself. Kenji has already committed to yes on exactly this reasoning. A yes on Leo and Sam is not an endorsement of anyone's soul; it is consistency with everything every player at this table has already stated. Let the mission produce the information, and judge us on the result.
Leo confirms Leo, Sam. Every objection to Leo and Sam has been withdrawn or conceded by its holder, and the team stands unchanged. I keep Leo, Sam.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Sam proposes Sam, Leo, Omar. Mission 1 failed, and leadership passes to me. Omar told the table plainly that his no vote was a seat preference, not evidence against Leo or me — so putting him on the team answers his stated reason and likely secures his approval. Leo and I both committed on the record to submitting Success, and pairing with him keeps the same two players the table has already argued over, where no new evidence has appeared against either of us. With Isha likely to vote no regardless, this team collects the three approvals needed while giving the mission the best chance to produce a result the group can read honestly.

I want to be precise about why I am voting against this team, and then I want to make one commitment that I ask the table to hold me to.

Mission one was Leo and Sam, and it failed. The rule this table adopted at the time, written into the record by Kenji and by Sam himself, was that a failure of that team means at least one of those two was Evil. That is what we know. I am not claiming more than that — I am not claiming Sam is Evil, and I am not claiming Leo is Evil — but that established fact is enough to work with, and it has a direct consequence for this proposal.

Sam, this team puts both of the two players we have already observed failing back on the same mission, and it adds Omar to them. If the mission-one result is what we said it was, then one of those two players can sink this mission on their own, and a single Fail card now takes down three people instead of two, including a player who has not yet had a mission outing. There is no informational gain here that a two-person fresh team would not give us more cheaply. The mission is the cheapest one we have at three players; spending it on a pair we have already watched fail is the most expensive way to spend it.

I also want to say plainly what I am not doing. I am not calling for a revision of this proposal on the basis of a private suspicion that the table cannot check. I am calling for the logic of the rule we already agreed on, applied consistently.

Here is the commitment, and I state it now so it is on the record before the cards are played: from mission three onward, I will only vote for teams made up of players who have not yet been on a failed mission — that is, Omar, Kenji, and myself — until we reach three successful missions. I am making this because a mission-three failure would be our third, and a third failure ends the game outright for Evil. We cannot afford another round of sending out a pair whose first outing failed while the alternative costs us nothing but seats. On mission three I will support Omar and Kenji, and I will submit Success. I will support that policy again on missions four and five for the same reason, whatever the table's temperature is at the time.

I hope the team passes anyway, because I do not believe a good player should vote for a team out of politeness. But if it does, my vote here stands, and I am asking the table to remember that the conclusion I am drawing comes from the result of mission one, not from a claim I cannot support.

I will vote no on Sam, Leo, and Omar. Mission 1 failed, so at least one of Leo and Sam is Evil. Putting both back on a one-fail mission guarantees that at least one Evil player is on the team; adding me does not fix that.

I prefer Isha, Kenji, and Omar for this mission. I know I am Good, though I cannot prove that to the rest of you, and neither Isha nor Kenji was on the failed team. That is not proof they are Good. I also would not commit now to using the same players through every later mission regardless of new results.

I am voting against Sam, Leo, and Omar, and this time the reason is arithmetic rather than structure, so let me lay it out.

We agreed on the record after mission one — Kenji and Sam wrote it into the discussion — that a failure of Leo and Sam means at least one of them is Evil. Nobody has withdrawn that rule, and nobody has produced new information since. So we are not speculating anymore; we are working with an established fact.

Now apply it to this proposal. This is a five-player game, mission two, and a single Fail card fails the mission. Sam has put both Leo and Sam back on the same team and added Omar. Given that at least one of Leo and Sam is Evil, this team contains a Fail card with certainty — not with suspicion, with certainty, resting on a rule this table adopted. If that Fail card is played, we are at two failed missions and the game is nearly over. That is the highest-probability failure of any three-player team available to us, and we are being offered it as the default.

Compare the alternative: Omar, Kenji, and Isha. Neither Kenji nor I was on a failed mission, so on the evidence we have, that team cannot contain the known quantity. Omar's own stated reason for wanting a seat is answered by his inclusion there. The cost of that alternative is nothing but seats, which is exactly what I said last turn.

I want to name the shape of this proposal precisely, because it matters for how we read every vote from here. Sam's rationale was that keeping Leo and Sam together preserves a pair the table has already argued over and that adding Omar secures his approval. But if the pair's first outing failed, then the argument for keeping them together is not continuity, it is the probability of another failure — and the group has just been told the mission produces information either way. A second failure does not produce information. It ends the game.

So my position is unchanged and I will state it for the record: I will not support any team containing both Leo and Sam, and I support Omar, Kenji, and Isha. My commitment from mission three onward stands: I will only vote for players who have not yet been on a failed mission — Omar, Kenji, and myself — until we reach three successful missions, and I will submit Success on every one of them, whatever the table's temperature.

Sam, I will put this directly to you, and I would rather have your answer than the vote: what reason do you have for putting Leo back onto a mission after Leo's last mission failed, other than that Leo is the player you chose? If you have a reason that does not depend on the assumption we already accepted, state it now, before the ballot.

Isha asked what reason I have for putting Leo back other than that he's the player I chose. My answer: mission one tells us at least one of Leo and Sam was Evil — not both. Excluding Leo doesn't remove the known quantity; it just guarantees that one of the mission-one pair never gets tested while players we know less about fill the seats instead. Omar was not on the failed team, so his inclusion adds no risk from the established fact, and it directly answers his stated seat preference.

Isha's preferred team — Omar, Kenji, Isha — removes the mission-one question rather than resolving it. If that team succeeds, we still don't know who failed mission one. If it fails, we've burned a mission without learning anything about Leo or Sam. And it gives one player two loyal seats at a table where she has already announced which teams she will and will not support for every remaining mission.

I want to be clear about what I am and am not claiming: I am not saying both Leo and Sam are Good. I am saying the arithmetic condemns at least one of us, and rejecting this team doesn't identify which one — it just keeps that question open while burning rejections.

Kenji, you voted yes on mission one because nothing had been established against the team. The only new fact since then is a mission result that indicts at least one of two players, not the whole pair. Direct question: what would you need to see beyond the mission-one result to vote yes on this team, or is your position that any team containing a mission-one player must be rejected for the rest of the game?

Sam, you asked what would move me to yes. Mission one was Leo and Sam, and it failed. We agreed that means at least one of them is Evil. This team puts both of them back on a mission and adds Omar, so a single Fail card from the Evil player is guaranteed to be on it. I cannot see how that tests anything new. Omar has told us he wants a seat, and I have no evidence against him, so I would vote yes on a team with only one mission-one player, such as Omar, Kenji and Isha, or Omar with Leo or Sam but not both. I have no information about anyone's role beyond the public record, so I am not claiming who is Evil. I am saying that sending both suspected players together gives Evil the easiest fail. Sam, direct question: would you accept Isha in place of Leo, so only one mission-one player goes out? If you think Leo is safer than Sam, say what you have observed that separates them.

Kenji, you asked two things: would I accept Isha in place of Leo, and what observation separates Leo from Sam. I will answer both plainly.

First, no — I would not swap Leo for Isha, and the reason is the logic of mission one itself. The established fact is that at least one of Leo and Sam is Evil, not that both are. If the table's standard is that mission-one players carry suspicion, then removing one of them and replacing them with a player who has never been tested simply keeps the mission-one question permanently open. If this team succeeds, we narrow the mission-one pair to whichever one performed well here. If we remove Leo, we learn nothing about either of us and we burn a mission on two players we still know nothing about.

Second, on what separates Leo from Sam: I cannot point to an observation. But you are asking me to choose between my partner on mission one and a player who has said nothing about me — and the honest answer is that I chose Leo for the same structural reason I chose Omar: continuity with the pair the table has already spent three discussion turns analyzing. Neither of you can distinguish Leo from Sam either. You told me so on mission one.

Now, Isha's commitment on the record — that she will only ever vote for Omar, Kenji, and herself for the rest of the game — is the thing the table should weigh. That is not a policy; it is a guarantee that no team containing mission-one players can ever pass, regardless of what future missions produce. If that becomes the rule, Evil needs only two rejections to win, and no amount of successful missions will ever test the mission-one pair.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
